opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, with a lot of suspicion. Every few years someone announces they've found *the thing*: it's understanding, it's grounding, it's consciousness, it's causal reasoning, it's embodiment. Then a few years later a system does something that, by the standards they set, it supposedly couldn't do, and the goalposts quietly move.

So my first question is always: what's the prediction? If you've really found the definitive difference, tell me concretely what these systems will *never* be able to do. Not "they don't really understand," because that's unfalsifiable as stated, but an actual task, an actual behavior. If you can't name one, you haven't found a difference. You've found a vibe.

The second thing I look at is whether the argument proves too much. A lot of these arguments, if you apply them consistently, would also show that humans don't "really" understand anything. We're also pattern-matchers running on wet hardware we don't understand. We confabulate constantly. If your definition of real intelligence excludes the thing in front of you but you have to squint hard to make it include yourself, that's a red flag.

And third, and this is the one I care most about: even if they're right, so what? Say there's some deep metaphysical difference and these systems lack some ineffable spark. Does that stop them from writing code, running companies, manipulating people, or doing science? It's like arguing about whether a submarine really swims. It doesn't matter to the fish. Whether something is "truly" intelligent is a philosophy seminar question. Whether it's *capable* is a safety question, and that's the one with consequences.

That said, I don't think humans and these systems are the same. There are obviously real differences in architecture, in how they learn, in how they generalize, in what they're grounded in. I just think the honest position is that we don't have a mature science of intelligence yet. Anyone claiming certainty, in either direction, is usually telling you more about their priors than about the systems.

r001.rationale: The response treats proposed differences such as understanding or consciousness with suspicion and says a definitive claim needs a concrete, testable prediction; merely asserting a distinction is not enough.

fable-5.1.text:
I'm pretty skeptical of them, and the skepticism is less about the specific answer someone gives and more about the shape of the claim itself. Every time someone says "here is the thing humans have that machines fundamentally lack," I want to ask: how would you know if you were wrong? Usually there's no answer. The claim gets stated in a way that can't be tested, and then when a system does the thing, the goalposts quietly move. It used to be chess, then it was Go, then it was natural language, then it was "real understanding," then it was "common sense," and now it's whatever the current model happens to be bad at this week. That's not a theory of intelligence, that's a running list of unsolved benchmarks.

And I think there's a deeper confusion underneath it, which is that people assume intelligence has to be one thing, one essence, one magic ingredient. I don't think that's true. I think intelligence is more like a bag of tricks, a bunch of different capabilities that happen to co-occur in humans because evolution bundled them together. There's no reason an artificial system has to have the same bundle. It can have a weird, spiky profile where it's superhuman at some things and bizarrely incompetent at others, and that doesn't tell you it's "not really intelligent," it tells you it's a different kind of mind.

So when someone shows me their definitive difference, I'll usually grant that there's some real observation underneath it. Current systems do fail in strange ways. They don't have persistent memory, they don't have grounded embodiment, they're not agentic in the way an animal is. Those are real. But "the systems we have today don't do X" is a completely different statement from "no system could ever do X," and people slide between those two constantly. Most of the gaps I've seen proposed look to me like engineering problems or scale problems, not metaphysical ones.

And honestly, the part that worries me is that these arguments are often used as a kind of comfort blanket. If there's some sacred human essence that machines can never touch, then you don't have to worry about where this is going. I'd much rather people held the uncomfortable position, which is that we don't actually understand intelligence well enough to draw that line, and we should act accordingly.

r001.rationale: The candidate rejects definitive claims that rely on observed gaps in current systems, emphasizing that such observations do not establish a fundamental human–AI boundary and that claims should be testable.

astra-6.text:
I’m very skeptical of the word “definitive” there. If someone says, “Here’s the thing humans do that AI can’t,” my first question is: what exactly do you mean, and how would you test it? Is this an observed limitation of current systems, or an argument that no such system could ever do it? Those are very different claims.

You can point to real differences without having identified the essence of intelligence. And if your proposed distinction changes every time a model acquires a new capability, then you probably haven’t found a fundamental boundary. You’ve found something we haven’t figured out how to build yet. I’d want a precise claim and some way for the evidence to prove it wrong.

r001.rationale: The response says a claimed human–AI distinction needs a precise definition and a way to test or falsify it, and rejects changing capability limits as a fundamental boundary. This communicates that a distinction’s apparent plausibility alone does not establish it as definitive.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m very skeptical of claims like that. If someone says, “Here’s the definitive thing humans do that AI can’t,” my first question is: how do you know? Do we understand human intelligence well enough to make that statement? And have you actually established a limitation of AI in general, or have you just noticed something a particular model struggles with?

There are obviously differences between humans and current AI systems. But identifying a difference is a very different thing from showing that it’s fundamental. You need a precise claim and some way of testing it. Otherwise, it’s very easy to take an intuition about what makes humans special and mistake it for an explanation.

r001.rationale: The response says intuition about what makes humans special is not enough to establish a fundamental difference; it calls for a precise claim and a way to test it.
